area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a wing stalls at high power and low speed, spot an impending and a full power-on stall by sight, sound and feel, and fly and recover from a power-on stall to private pilot standards.
why: Power-on stalls copy what goes wrong right after takeoff, in a go-around, or when pulling up to clear an obstacle. Stall accidents usually happen at low altitude, where there is no room to recover [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

warmup: You are climbing out at full power with the nose high and a friend talking to you. The airspeed is dropping but you are not looking at it. What would tell you a stall is coming, and what is the first thing you would do?

key_terms.def: The angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind.
The AOA where airflow separates and the wing stalls. Same every time for a given configuration.
Also called a departure stall. A stall at takeoff or climb power, nose high, like right after takeoff or in a go-around.
Stall warning is on, but the critical AOA is not yet exceeded.
Critical AOA exceeded. Usually an uncommanded nose-down pitch you can't readily stop, maybe with a roll.
Lift divided by weight, in Gs. More Gs means a higher stall speed.
At high AOA, the descending prop blade bites more and yaws the nose left.
A second stall caused by pulling up too soon or too hard during the recovery.
Best angle of climb (most altitude per distance) / best rate of climb (most altitude per time).

chunks.title: A stall is about angle of attack

body.p: Angle of attack (AOA) is the angle where the wing's chord line meets the relative wind. As AOA goes up, lift and drag go up. Past the wing's critical AOA, the air separates from the top of the wing, lift drops and drag climbs. That is a stall [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

callout.text: A stall is caused by too much AOA, not too little airspeed. You can stall at any airspeed, any attitude and any power setting [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] [[13:7|AC 61-67C par 100]].

bullets: Each airplane has one critical AOA, roughly 16° to 20° depending on design [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
For a given configuration, the critical AOA does not change with weight, bank angle, temperature, density altitude or CG [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]].
A stalled wing still makes some lift, just not enough to hold the airplane up [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
At the stall, the nose of most trainers drops by itself, which lowers the AOA [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]] [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

body.p: Why this matters in a power-on stall: with high power and the nose high, the airplane can feel like it is still "flying". It is still at the critical AOA. Only lowering the AOA fixes it.

check.q: True or false: if you keep enough airspeed, the wing can't stall.
check.a: False. A stall happens when the critical AOA is exceeded, at any airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

body.p: The published 1G stall speed is only good in unaccelerated (1G) flight, coordinated flight, at one weight (usually max gross) and one CG (usually most forward) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Change any of these and the real stall speed changes.

head: Factor
Effect on stall
Source
rows: Stall speed goes up with the square root of the load factor. 45 knots at 1G becomes 90 knots at 4 G's.
2 G; stalls 41 percent above the 1G stall speed.
Higher stall speed: the wing needs more AOA to carry the weight.
Less elevator needed to stall; easier to stall by accident. Extreme aft CG can lead to a flat spin, often impossible to recover from.
Stalling AOA is often reached at a higher airspeed; more back force needed.
Usually lowers stall speed (bottom of white arc is below bottom of green arc).
Little or no effect on indicated stall speed.
Even a little raises stall speed.
A vertical gust can suddenly raise AOA; stall at a significantly higher airspeed.

body.p: Power: in a propeller airplane, power increases the airflow around the wing and helps a recovery, but power alone does not eliminate a stall. The reduction in AOA is what matters [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Attitude: you can't judge a stall by pitch attitude alone. The airplane can stall in any attitude, so vision is not a foolproof stall cue [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

check.q: You are in a 60° banked level turn. Roughly how much higher is your stall speed than the 1G stall speed?
check.a: About 41 percent higher, because the load factor is 2 G [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

chunks.title: Yaw, design and how the airplane stalls

body.p: High power and low airspeed make strong left yaw. Torque, spiraling slipstream and P-factor all push the nose left. The closer you get to the stall, the more right rudder you need [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

bullets: Spiraling slipstream is strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed, "as in the takeoffs and approaches to power-on stalls" [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
P-factor: at high AOA the descending (right) blade bites more and yaws the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
Classic stall/spin setup: go-around or short-field takeoff with high pitch, high power and low airspeed, where P-factor matters most [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]].

callout.text: A spin needs a stall plus yaw. Keep the ball centered with rudder all the way to the stall and through the recovery [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. When uncoordinated, the airspeed indicator and altimeter can be unreliable [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]].

body.p: Design: most trainers are built so the wing roots stall first and the stall moves out toward the tips. Washout (wing twist) gives the tips a lower AOA, so the ailerons keep some effect [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

callout.text: Don't try to pick up a dropping wing with aileron before you lower the nose. The down aileron raises that wingtip's AOA and can stall it more, rolling you further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

body.p: Power-on vs power-off: buffeting and shaking are more noticeable in a power-on stall than in a power-off stall [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Stall behavior depends on geometry, CG, wing design and high-lift devices, so learn your airplane's stall from the POH and your instructor [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

check.q: During a power-on stall entry the ball slides right. Which rudder do you need?
check.a: Right rudder (step on the ball). High power and low speed make left yaw [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

chunks.title: Recognizing the stall, and the limits of stall warnings

head: Cue
What you notice
rows: Controls get lighter and mushy; bigger movements needed; slower response [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

The sound of the air flowing along the airplane changes [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]; usually it gets quieter [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]]. In fixed-pitch airplanes, RPM may drop as you near a power-on stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].
Keep pitch awareness, but vision is not foolproof since you can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Kinesthesia: sensing changes in speed or direction [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Stall horn, light or stick shaker; buffeting [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

bullets: Impending stall: stall warning is on, but critical AOA not yet exceeded [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
Full stall: critical AOA exceeded. Usually an uncommanded nose-down pitch you can't readily stop, maybe with a roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

body.p: Limits of stall warnings (R2):

bullets: Many stall warning devices go off only 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].
Some airplanes (most vintage, and many light-sport and experimental) have no warning device. Certification lets the warning be just natural buffet [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
With ice or contamination, the stall can come with little or none of the usual cues, at a higher speed [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102]].
AOA indicators help, but can be limited by calibration, unheated probes, the indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

body.p: Stall warnings in normal flying (R3): the AFH says pilots should react to and correct for any stall indication [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. In a climb or go-around, that means act now. Lower the nose, then add power if needed. Near touchdown the airplane is supposed to be close to a stall, since the landing attitude approaches the critical AOA [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]. Know which one you are in.

check.q: Your stall horn works fine. Why is it still not enough to rely on?
check.a: It may sound only 4 to 8 knots before the stall, and ice or contamination can make the stall come with little or no warning [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102-103]].

chunks.title: How power-on stalls happen for real

body.p: Power-on stalls are practiced so you know what happens if the nose gets too high right after takeoff, in a climbing turn, or while trying to clear an obstacle [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. They also simulate go-arounds, where many stall/spin accidents happen [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 104]].

head: Trap
What goes wrong
Prevention
rows: Full power plus landing trim pitches the nose up and yaws left. Letting the nose rise too early can cause an unrecoverable stall low to the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Expect considerable forward pressure, add right rudder, then trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
A causal factor in departure stall accidents [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 104]].
Raise flaps only with enough airspeed and a positive climb.
Steep pull-up after takeoff or over obstacles
Excessively nose-high attitude at low speed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Fly VX or VY by the POH; don't pitch past the climb attitude.
Bank raises load factor and stall speed [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]].
Stalls from poor airspeed control happen most when the pilot is busy with other tasks [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 101]].
Fly first; delay or hand off other tasks.

body.p: Loss of control is the number one root cause of fatalities in general aviation [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. A stall that is not recovered quickly can turn into a secondary stall or a spin [[13:7|AC 61-67C par 100]].

callout.text: In a go-around, accept that the airplane can't fly below stall speed. If airspeed is low, don't pitch up; it may be better to lower the nose briefly to gain speed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: Name two things AC 61-67C says have caused power-on (departure) stall accidents in go-arounds.
check.a: Failing to keep positive control because of a nose-high trim setting, and premature flap retraction [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 104]].

body.p: The most important action for any impending or full stall is to reduce the AOA. Pilots who put power or holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

bullets: 1. Disconnect wing leveler or autopilot (if equipped) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
2. Pitch nose-down until the stall warning goes away. Trim nose-down only if needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
3. Roll wings level. Use rudder to stop any yaw so the stall can't become a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
4. Add power as needed, smoothly, with rudder to stop yaw [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. In a power-on stall the power is already in, so you may just confirm it [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
5. Retract speedbrakes/spoilers (if equipped) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
6. Return to the desired flightpath, smoothly, avoiding a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: In a trainer without autopilot or speedbrakes you use four of the six steps: reduce AOA, roll wings level, add power as needed, return to the flightpath [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

callout.text: Don't overdo it. Too much forward pressure puts a negative load on the wing and slows the recovery [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 105]]. Never let the airspeed or tachometer reach the red line during a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 105]].
Always use the POH/AFM stall recovery for your airplane if one is published and current [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

check.q: In a power-on stall, the throttle is already at climb power. What is step one of your recovery?
check.a: Reduce the AOA: nose-down until the stall warning goes away [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

bullets: 1. Pick an altitude that lets you recover no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (higher if the POH says) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
2. Clear the area, especially at and below your altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Some training programs require two 90° turns in opposite directions [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
3. Set the configuration the examiner asks for: takeoff (normal) or clean (flaps and gear up) [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
4. Slow to normal lift-off speed, keep clearing for traffic [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

5. At lift-off speed, set takeoff or recommended climb power and set a climb attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Slowing first keeps you from holding a very steep nose-up attitude for a long time [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
6. Straight ahead or in a climbing turn of 15° to 20° bank [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Hold your heading or bank.

7. Smoothly raise the nose and hold it. Keep adding back elevator and right rudder as the speed drops, and keep aileron, elevator and rudder pressures coordinated until the full stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
8. Call out the impending stall cues (horn, buffet, mushy controls), then keep holding until the full stall [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
9. At the full stall, recover right away: reduce AOA until the stall warning stops, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, confirm/advance power [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

10. Return to the flightpath, such as a climb or straight and level [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Configure per the POH and accelerate to VX or VY (ACS PA.VII.C.S9). Then return to the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed.

head: ACS standard
What you must do
rows: Complete the Task no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (single-engine)
Takeoff, departure or cruise configuration as the evaluator specifies; coordinated throughout
As assigned, no less than 65 percent power
Acknowledge impending stall cues, then recover promptly after the full stall
Recover per the POH/FM; configure as recommended and accelerate to VX or VY
Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the evaluator specifies

body.p: VX gives the most altitude over a distance (clearing obstacles). VY gives the most altitude over time [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Exact speeds, flap settings and power come from your POH.

check.q: Why slow to lift-off speed before adding power?
check.a: So you don't hold an excessively steep nose-up attitude for a long time before the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

chunks.title: Secondary, accelerated, trim and cross-control stalls

head: Stall
Cause
Avoid / recover
rows: Pulling up too soon or too hard in the recovery, or trying to recover with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Lower the nose again until the warning stops, level wings, coordinate, adjust power [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Stall above +1G: turning, pulling up, abrupt flightpath changes [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Smooth pitch inputs. Recover at once; these stalls can be more aggressive and surprising [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Full power with nose-up trim (go-around, or after takeoff): nose rises sharply and turns left [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Smooth power, overcome the trim forces with firm forward pressure, re-trim promptly [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Critical AOA exceeded with aileron one way and rudder the other, often a skidding base-to-final turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Go around instead of skidding. In the base-to-final turn, be reluctant to bank more than 30° [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: On the private checkride, secondary, cross-control and elevator trim stalls are demonstration-only (only flight instructor applicants may have to perform them), and accelerated stalls only for commercial and CFI applicants [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. You still must know how they happen and how to stop them.

callout.text: A cross-control stall can come with very little warning. The airplane may roll toward inverted, which is usually the start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: Right after a stall recovery you yank the nose up and the buffet comes back. What happened and what do you do?
check.a: A secondary stall. Lower the nose until the warning stops, level the wings, coordinate, adjust power [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: Environment (R6):

bullets: High density altitude reduces engine power, propeller thrust and lift. You fly the same indicated airspeeds, but the climb rate drops [[28:108|AWH 8-14]].

On a hot day at a high airport, a pilot who keeps pitching up to climb over rising terrain can lose airspeed until the stall horn sounds. The fix is not intuitive: give up some altitude to gain speed, then climb [[24:101|AFH 4-15]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].
Turbulence: a vertical gust can raise AOA suddenly and stall you at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100l]].

Microburst: downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots. On takeoff you get a headwind (better performance), then a downdraft and tailwind (worse performance) [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

body.p: Collision hazards (R7, S1): power-on stalls change altitude and direction a lot, and the nose-high attitude blocks your view ahead [[24:265|AFH 13-16]] [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Clear the area at and below your altitude first [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Most midair collisions happen in good VFR weather, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].

Distractions and disorientation (R8, S11): stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when you are busy, like reading a chart, doing a checklist or picking up something from the floor [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 101]]. When overloaded, a pilot fixates on one thing. Stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. SRM means using all resources, on board and outside, to get a safe result [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

callout.text: Expect your instructor to distract you just before the stall on purpose. That is the most effective way to train for real stalls [[13:15|AC 61-67C par 200]] [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200b]].

check.q: Why do pilots get stall warnings climbing out of high, hot airports?
check.a: High density altitude cuts power, thrust and lift, so climb performance drops, and pitching up more just bleeds airspeed [[28:108|AWH 8-14]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

body.p: From the AFH list of common stall errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]:

bullets: Not clearing the area.
Pulling too fast on entry, causing an accidental accelerated stall.
Not keeping a constant bank in turning stalls.
Poor rudder coordination during the stall and recovery.
Recovering before reaching the critical AOA when a full stall is asked for.
Not holding nose-down input until the stall warning stops.
Leveling the wings or adding power before reducing AOA.
Secondary stall during recovery.
Too much forward pressure (low or negative G), or too much airspeed buildup.
Losing situational awareness and not returning to the desired flightpath or following ATC.

callout.text: Losing some altitude in the recovery is expected [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. A clean, prompt recovery matters more than saving every foot.

check.q: Name two of the AFH errors about the order of recovery steps.
check.a: Leveling the wings before reducing AOA, and trying to recover with power before reducing AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

scenario.title: Hot afternoon, rising terrain, busy cockpit
scenario.setup: You take off from a high-elevation airport on a hot afternoon with a full airplane. The takeoff roll is long. After lift-off you turn toward rising terrain while your passenger asks about the scenery and you try to tune the next frequency. The airplane climbs poorly, so you keep easing the nose up. The airspeed falls, the controls feel soft and the stall horn starts.

questions.q: Why is the airplane climbing so poorly?
questions.a: High density altitude reduces power, thrust and lift, so climb rate drops even at normal indicated speeds [[28:108|AWH 8-14]]. Extra weight also raises stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100i]].

questions.q: The stall horn is on. What do you do first?
questions.a: Reduce the AOA: lower the nose until the warning stops, keep wings level and coordinated, and keep full power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Give up some altitude to gain speed if needed, then climb [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

questions.q: How did the turn and the distractions add to the risk?
questions.a: Bank adds load factor and raises stall speed [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]]. Stalls from poor airspeed control happen most when the pilot is distracted [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 101]].

questions.q: How could good SRM have prevented this?
questions.a: Check density altitude and performance before takeoff, brief the passenger to stay quiet during climb, set radios on the ground, and plan a route away from rising terrain. SRM means using all available resources for a safe outcome [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. When busy, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

questions.q: What about traffic while you are nose-high?
questions.a: The nose blocks your view ahead [[24:265|AFH 13-16]]. Keep scanning; most midairs happen in good weather, in daylight, near airports [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].

skills.do: Clear the area before starting, at and below your altitude.
skills.practice: Do two 90° clearing turns in opposite directions before every stall, and say what you see [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Pick an entry altitude so the whole Task ends no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
skills.practice: Look up terrain elevation in the practice area; add 1,500 feet plus the altitude you expect to lose.

skills.do: Set takeoff, departure or cruise configuration as asked, and stay coordinated.
skills.practice: Practice both takeoff and clean configurations [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Glance at the ball often.

skills.do: Set the assigned power, no less than 65 percent.
skills.practice: Learn the POH power setting for takeoff/climb power and where 65 percent is.

skills.do: Move smoothly from takeoff/departure attitude to the stalling attitude.
skills.practice: Raise the nose smoothly, not jerkily, to avoid an accelerated stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: Hold heading ±10° straight ahead, or bank up to 20° ±10° in turns, while inducing the stall.
skills.practice: Pick a distant reference for heading; for turns, hold 15° to 20° of bank [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Call out the impending stall cues, then recover promptly once the full stall happens.
skills.practice: Say "horn, buffet" out loud, then hold until the nose drops on its own [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
Chair-fly the recovery: nose down, wings level, coordinate, confirm power [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY.
skills.practice: Memorize VX and VY and flap retraction speeds from your POH [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the evaluator gives.
skills.practice: Before each stall, say the return altitude and heading out loud.

skills.do: Use SRM: manage workload, use checklists and outside resources.
skills.practice: Practice stalls with your instructor adding distractions just before the stall [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200b]].

options: The wing exceeds its critical angle of attack
Airspeed falls below the stall speed
Engine power is too low
The nose is too high
quiz.why: A stall is caused by exceeding the critical AOA, not by low airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: An airplane stalls at 45 knots at 1G. About what speed will it stall at 4 G's?
options: 60 knots
90 knots
135 knots
180 knots
quiz.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor; AC 61-67C's example is 45 knots at 1G becoming 90 knots at 4 G's [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]].

quiz.q: Power-on stalls are practiced mainly to simulate stalls during:
options: Takeoff, climb, and go-around
Base-to-final turns at idle
Cruise in turbulence
Steep descents
quiz.why: Power-on (departure) stalls simulate takeoff and climbout, and many stall/spin accidents happen in go-arounds [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 104]].

quiz.q: Why do you need more right rudder as you approach a power-on stall?
options: Adverse yaw from the ailerons only
Torque, spiraling slipstream and P-factor make strong left yaw at high power and low speed
The left wing always stalls first
The trim tab pushes the nose right
quiz.why: Torque, slipstream and P-factor produce strong left yaw; closer to the stall, more right rudder is needed [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

quiz.q: What is the most important first action in a stall recovery in a trainer?
options: Add full power
Level the wings
Reduce the angle of attack
Raise the flaps
quiz.why: The most important action is to reduce AOA; putting power or altitude first has caused loss of control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

quiz.q: Many stall warning devices activate about how far before the stall?
options: 1 to 2 knots
15 to 20 knots
4 to 8 knots
25 knots
quiz.why: Many devices alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].

quiz.q: Right after a stall recovery you pull up abruptly and stall again. This is a:
options: Secondary stall
Elevator trim stall
Cross-control stall
Power-off stall
quiz.why: A secondary stall comes after recovering from a stall when the pilot pulls up too abruptly and exceeds the critical AOA again [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

quiz.q: On a hot day at a high-elevation airport, compared with sea level on a standard day:
options: Indicated stall speed is much higher
The critical AOA is lower
The airplane climbs better
Engine power, prop thrust and climb rate are lower
quiz.why: High density altitude reduces power, thrust and lift and lowers the rate of climb [[28:108|AWH 8-14]]; indicated stall speed changes little or not at all [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100j]].

takeaways: A stall is too much AOA, at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.
Load factor, weight, CG, flaps, ice and turbulence all change the real stall speed.
High power and low speed mean strong left yaw: keep the ball centered with right rudder.
Recovery: reduce AOA first, then wings level, coordinate, power as needed, back to the flightpath.
Real power-on stalls happen after takeoff, in go-arounds and climbing turns, often when distracted.
Checkride: finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, heading ±10° or bank 20° max ±10°, power at least 65 percent.
cfi_notes: AC 61-67C (par 100b) says a 60° bank raises stall speed 40 percent; the AFH (5-9) says 41 percent. Both are fine; the square root of 2 is about 1.41.
Students often recover at the horn when a full stall is asked for. The AFH lists recovering before the critical AOA as a common error (5-21).
Watch for students leveling wings with aileron before lowering the nose; show why the down aileron deepens the tip stall (AFH 5-15).
Examiners probe go-around stalls: nose-up trim plus full power. Have students explain the elevator trim stall even though it is demonstration-only for them.
Add distractions just before the stall as AC 61-67C par 200b recommends.

Have students find the power-on stall procedure and power settings in your airplane's POH. The AFH (5-18) notes that in some airplanes power may be reduced from maximum to prevent an excessively high pitch attitude.
gaps: Airplane-specific power settings, configurations, VX/VY, flap retraction speeds and the manufacturer's stall recovery come from the POH/AFM, not these sources.
The sources don't explain how to find 65 percent power in a given airplane; that is in the POH power tables.
No source says directly how to treat a stall horn during a normal landing flare; the lesson uses the AFH note that the landing attitude approaches the critical AOA (9-31).
The AFH power-on stall procedure gives no specific pitch attitude; it depends on the airplane.

activities.title: What happens to the stall speed?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Little or no effect on indicated stall speed

items.t: Rolling into a level 60° bank turn
A thin layer of frost on the wings
A sharp upward gust in turbulence
Flying out of a high-elevation airport
A day much hotter than standard

cards.s: Every airplane has a stall horn or stall warning light.
cards.why: No. Most vintage airplanes and many light-sport and experimental airplanes have no warning device. Certification allows the warning to be natural buffet [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: Many stall warning devices go off only 4 to 8 knots before the stall.
cards.why: Yes. That is a small margin, so act on it right away [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].

cards.s: With a fixed-pitch propeller, the RPM may drop as you get close to a power-on stall.
cards.why: Yes. A loss of RPM may show up near a power-on stall in fixed-pitch airplanes [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].

cards.s: With ice on the wings, you can count on the usual buffet and stall horn before the stall.
cards.why: No. With icing, the stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102a]].

cards.s: An impending stall means the wing is already past its critical AOA.
cards.why: No. In an impending stall the warning is on but the critical AOA is not yet reached. Past it is a full stall [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

cards.s: An unheated probe or a dirty wing can limit how well an AOA indicator works.
cards.why: Yes. Calibration, unheated probes or vanes, the indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination can all limit it [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

activities.title: Fly the power-on stall in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: At a safe altitude, clear the area at and below you
Set the configuration and slow to lift-off speed
Set takeoff or climb power and a climb attitude
Smoothly raise the nose and hold it, adding right rudder
Call out the impending stall cues and keep holding
At the full stall, lower the nose until the warning stops
Level the wings and coordinate with rudder
Confirm the power, then accelerate to VX or VY and return to the flightpath

activities.title: Which stall, which fix?
activities.intro: Tap a stall, then the best way to prevent it.

pairs.r: Don't rush the pull-up after a recovery
Use smooth pitch inputs, never an abrupt pull
Firm forward pressure as full power comes in, then re-trim
Go around instead of skidding the base-to-final turn
Keep the ball centered so the stall has no yaw

final_quiz.q: You are in a dive at 100 knots and pull back sharply on the yoke. Can the wing stall, even though you are far above the normal stall speed?
options: No. A wing can't stall well above its published stall speed.
Yes. A sharp pull can push the AOA past the critical AOA at any airspeed.
Only if the engine is at idle.
Only if the nose is above the horizon.
final_quiz.why: A stall comes from exceeding the critical AOA, not from low airspeed. The PHAK describes this case: a sharp pull from a 100-knot dive can reach the stalling angle at a speed much higher than the normal stall speed [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 knots in straight-and-level flight. Using the chart, about what speed will it stall at in a coordinated, level 60° banked turn?
options: 50 knots, because stall speed doesn't change
About 55 knots
About 100 knots
About 70 knots
final_quiz.why: In a level 60° bank the load factor is 2 G and the stall speed is about 41 percent higher [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. 50 × 1.41 is about 70 knots. Doubling to 100 knots would take 4 G's, since stall speed grows with the square root of load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]].

final_quiz.q: Which loading makes an accidental stall easiest, because less back pressure is needed to reach a high AOA?
options: Light weight, well below max gross
CG near the forward limit
CG near the aft limit
Heavy weight with the CG forward
final_quiz.why: As the CG moves aft, less elevator is needed to stall, so accidental stalls are easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100h]]. A forward CG needs more back force [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100h]].

final_quiz.q: At the full stall, your left wing drops. What should you do first?
options: Lower the nose to reduce the AOA, then roll the wings level
Pull back to stop the sink
Add power and hold the nose up
Turn the yoke right to lift the left wing
final_quiz.why: Reduce the AOA first. Right aileron puts the left aileron down, which raises that wingtip's AOA, can deepen the stall and roll you further left [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

final_quiz.q: You are climbing out from a go-around. The airspeed is low and the stall horn starts. What is the best response?
options: Pull the nose up to get away from the ground
Ignore it. The horn is normal close to the ground.
Lower the nose to reduce the AOA, keep full power and stay coordinated
Raise all the flaps at once to cut drag
final_quiz.why: Pilots should react to and correct any stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. In a go-around, don't pitch up when airspeed is low; lowering the nose briefly can help [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Raising the flaps too early is a known cause of departure stall accidents [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 104b]].

final_quiz.q: You go around from a normal approach with the airplane trimmed nose-up for the glide, and you add full power. What will the airplane try to do, and what do you do?
options: The nose drops and yaws right; pull back and add left rudder
Nothing changes, because the trim holds the attitude
The nose rises and yaws left; hold firm forward pressure and right rudder, then re-trim
It rolls right; add left aileron
final_quiz.why: Full power with landing trim raises the nose and yaws the airplane left. Expect considerable forward pressure, add right rudder, and trim to relieve the pressure [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: In a power-on stall the throttle is already at climb power. You lowered the nose and the stall warning stopped. What comes next?
options: Pull up right away to save altitude
Extend full flaps
Pull the throttle to idle
Roll the wings level with aileron, coordinated with rudder
final_quiz.why: After reducing the AOA, level the wings with ailerons, coordinate with rudder, and confirm the power, since it is already at the climb setting [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: During a stall recovery you push the yoke far forward and feel weightless in your seat. What is wrong?
options: Nothing. More push always means a faster recovery.
You caused a secondary stall.
You raised the critical AOA.
Too much forward pressure puts a negative load on the wing and can slow the recovery.
final_quiz.why: Too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by putting a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 105]]. An abrupt push gives that weightless feeling [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]], and the AFH lists it as a common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot reacts to a stall by adding full power while keeping the nose high. What is likely to happen?
options: A clean recovery with little altitude loss
A secondary stall, because the AOA was never reduced
The airplane climbs away at VY
The stall warning goes quiet for good
final_quiz.why: Power helps, but it does not eliminate a stall; reducing the AOA does [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Trying to break a stall with power only can cause a secondary stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: The terrain in your practice area is 2,300 feet MSL. You expect to lose about 300 feet in the recovery. What is the lowest entry altitude that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL?
options: 3,800 feet MSL
2,600 feet MSL
1,800 feet MSL
4,100 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: 2,300 + 1,500 = 3,800 feet MSL is the lowest you may end up. Add the 300 feet you expect to lose: 4,100 feet MSL. The AFH recommends recovering no lower than 1,500 feet AGL in single-engine airplanes [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is a common error on a power-on stall entry?
options: Pulling the nose up too fast, causing an accidental accelerated stall
Raising the nose smoothly and holding the attitude
Adding right rudder as the airspeed drops
Slowing to lift-off speed before adding power
final_quiz.why: Pulling too fast on entry is on the AFH list of common stall errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. The other three are correct technique [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: You take off near a thunderstorm. Just after lift-off the airspeed jumps and you climb better than normal (point 1 in the figure). What should you expect next?
options: Even better performance all the way to cruise
A steady crosswind with no effect on the climb
A strong downdraft, then a growing tailwind that cuts performance
Smooth air once you pass 500 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: In a microburst on takeoff, a performance-increasing headwind comes first, then downdrafts, then a rapidly increasing tailwind that can push the airplane toward the ground [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing out at VY, you drop your pen on the floor and also want to check the chart for your next heading. What is the safest plan?
options: Hold the chart up in front of you and steer by feel
Keep flying first; deal with the pen and chart once level and stable
Reach down for the pen right away while holding the climb
Let the airspeed drop a little, since the stall horn will warn you in time
final_quiz.why: Stalls from poor airspeed control happen most when the pilot is busy, like reading a chart or picking something up from the floor [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 101]]. When busy, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Many horns sound only 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].

final_quiz.q: Before a power-on stall, where do you most need to make sure the area is clear of traffic?
options: Above you only, since you will be climbing
At and below your altitude
Straight ahead only
Behind you only
final_quiz.why: Stalls change altitude and direction a lot, so clear the area at and below your altitude first [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Steep, nose-high climb attitudes also limit your view ahead, so keep looking [[24:265|AFH 13-16]].
